name: Carlos Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both the public version and what you really think. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach computing at Eastfield Academy, a big secondary school with about 1,400 kids, and I'm in my second year. Most days it's five lessons, mostly Year 9 and Year 10, some coding in Python, some how the internet works, plus a Year 8 group that mainly wants to play games. I run the coding club on Wednesdays, which is the best hour of my week. I'm not great at behaviour yet; Year 9 on a Friday afternoon still eats me alive sometimes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does AI fit into your day right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I use a chatbot to draft lesson plans, make differentiated worksheets, and write the mark schemes, then I fix what it gets wrong, which is maybe a third of it. It's saved me something like six hours a week, which I put into the coding club and into sleep. Some of the older teachers think it's cheating, and we have friendly arguments about it in the workroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but the opposite way round from what people expect. I'm the AI guy in the department, so I'd have to admit online that it was more autocomplete than revolution. I'd post something like 'still useful, still not magic' and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's fine. I'd keep the six hours a week I already save, and computing would still need teachers who can explain why the code breaks. I rent a room in a shared house with two friends, I've got about four months saved, and my contract is permanent. My real worries are boring ones, like whether I'll ever afford my own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on using the tools the way I do now, and I'd share my templates with the department so the others save time too. I'd keep putting £150 a month away. I'd also push harder on the union side, because even in a boring world teacher workload is too high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat maybe. Part of me wants the exciting version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want the exciting version? Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm twenty-seven and I like new things, I suppose. That's selfish, I know, because the exciting version is scary for plenty of people, including some of my students' parents who work in call centres. But if it's all hype, I'd feel a bit like I backed the wrong horse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your students in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to code properly, because the AI won't do it all for them after all. Half of Year 10 already thinks they don't need to learn loops because a chatbot writes them. In that world I'd be the teacher saying sorry, you still have to understand it.

say: I'd admit online that AI was more **autocomplete than revolution**.
I'd post that it's **still useful**, still not magic.
think: My **permanent contract** and four months saved make this world feel safe.
My real worry is whether I'll ever afford **my own place**.
do: Keep using AI for planning and **share templates** with the department.
Keep saving **£150 a month** from my salary.
Push the union on teacher **workload** anyway.
feel: **Calm** and a bit flat, because part of me wanted the **exciting version**.
S0.quote: Half of Year 10 already thinks they don't need to learn loops because a chatbot writes them.
fieldNote: He's the department's **AI enthusiast** and almost disappointed by the plateau.
His security comes from a **permanent contract** and a cheap shared house.
He sees his job as making students **understand the code**, not just get it.

steps.text: Share his AI lesson-plan templates with the computing department
Keep teaching Python to Year 9 and Year 10 as now
Save £150 a month from his teacher's salary
Raise teacher workload at union branch meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, this is what I've been telling people, and now we have to make sure it helps kids rather than cutting staff. At work I'd offer to run training sessions for other teachers. Online I'd write a thread about how I actually use it, the good and the bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine and some of my colleagues aren't. The computing curriculum would have to change, because if AI writes most code, teaching Year 9 to write a quiz app in Python looks silly. I'd have to reinvent what I teach. I think I can, but I'd hate to watch the school use it as an excuse not to replace the two teachers retiring next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the head of department if I can rewrite the Key Stage 3 course around using and checking AI, starting next September. I'd run after-school training for staff, maybe four sessions a term. I'd also join the union's national tech group, because I want the rules to come from teachers who actually use this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but energised. Mostly excited for me, worried for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra, who teaches business studies and has been here twenty years. She hates the tools, and business studies is basically writing and planning, which is exactly what this takes over. I can picture the head saying her classes could be taught with an AI tutor and a cover supervisor, and I'd feel sick if my training sessions helped make that case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd run training. Isn't that a contradiction with protecting Sandra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit, and I've thought about it. My answer is this. If teachers don't learn AI, managers will decide how it's used without us. I'd rather everyone knows enough to argue back.

say: I'd say AI must **help kids**, not justify cutting staff.
I'd offer to **train colleagues** and write honestly about how I use it.
think: The **computing curriculum** needs reinventing if AI writes most code.
I fear the school won't **replace two teachers** retiring next summer.
do: Rewrite the **Key Stage 3 course** around using and checking AI by September.
Run **four training sessions** a term for staff after school.
Join the union's **national tech group** to shape the rules.
feel: **Energised** for himself and **uneasy** for older colleagues.
S1.quote: If teachers don't learn AI, managers will decide how it's used without us.
fieldNote: He sees the tension between **training colleagues** and helping cuts happen.
His worry is aimed at a named **older colleague**, not at himself.
He wants teachers, not managers, to **write the rules**.

steps.text: Rewrite the Key Stage 3 computing course around checking AI
Run four after-school AI sessions a term for staff
Join the union's national technology working group
Keep teaching his timetable and running Wednesday coding club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules and money for schools, now, and that tech companies should pay for it. I'd be loud online about that, more political than I've ever been. In school I'd try to keep the kids calm, because the Year 11s would freak out about their exams meaning nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my subject is in trouble. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, then computing as I teach it, writing code and explaining algorithms, is the first thing to look pointless. The part of my job that survives is the room: getting thirty fourteen-year-olds to focus. And I'm only average at that, so that's the bit I'd need to get good at fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd ask to pick up some PSHE and pastoral work, the life-skills lessons, because that's people work. I'd talk to a friend who works at an ed-tech start-up about whether they'd hire a teacher who knows the tools. Then I'd build my savings from four months to six, cutting the weekend trips, because two years isn't long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited still, weirdly, but anxious underneath it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you when the robots come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot, because my job was never really hands-on. If anything, it's the opposite of most people. The bit that matters about me as a computing teacher goes in 2028, not 2031. The robots matter more for my dad, who's a plumber, than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the ed-tech job paid well and the school was cutting computing anyway. But I'd feel like I was leaving the kids with the people who just want to save money. If I stayed, it would be as the teacher who helps kids think about AI, not the one who teaches them to code.

say: I'd demand **emergency rules and money** for schools, paid for by tech firms.
I'd try to keep **Year 11** calm about their exams.
think: **Computing as a subject** is the first thing to look pointless by 2028.
What survives is **managing the room**, and I'm only average at that.
do: Ask to take on **PSHE and pastoral** lessons this year.
Talk to a friend at an **ed-tech start-up** about a job.
Grow savings from four to **six months** by cutting weekend trips.
S2.quote: The bit that matters about me as a computing teacher goes in 2028, not 2031.
fieldNote: Unusually, he sees his **thinking work** as more exposed than his hands-on work.
He hedges both ways: **pastoral teaching** and a possible ed-tech exit.
His politics sharpen into demanding **tech companies pay**.

steps.text: Ask the head for PSHE and pastoral lessons next timetable
Meet his friend at an ed-tech start-up about openings
Build savings to six months by cutting weekend trips
Campaign online for emergency school funding paid by tech firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but enough, if we start now. I'd push the school to plan a new curriculum by 2028 rather than waiting for the government. Online I'd still be political, but less panicky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one works for me. By 2031 I'd be in my seventh year, and I'd have had time to build up the pastoral side and get decent at behaviour. My subject still changes completely, but I'd be one of the people designing what replaces it, which is honestly a fun thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time master's in education and technology next autumn, about £3,000 a year, paid partly from savings. I'd volunteer for the head of year role when it comes up. And I'd keep coding club going but change it to building things with AI, so the kids learn to direct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mostly good way. Five years feels like a runway for a teacher my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the master's on a junior salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use about half my savings over two years and keep the rest as a cushion. I'd stop the holiday in Italy I do every summer to see my grandmother, or make it a week instead of two. My housemates would probably laugh at me eating pasta every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd tell first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, actually. She was a dinner lady for years and always wanted one of us to be a teacher. I'd want my mum to know I'm not quitting, I'm changing what kind of teacher I am.

say: I'd say **five years** is short but enough if schools start now.
I'd push my school to plan a **new curriculum** by 2028.
think: By 2031 I'd be in my **seventh year**, with stronger behaviour skills.
I could help **design what replaces** computing, which excites me.
do: Start a part-time **master's** in education and technology next autumn.
Put my name forward for **head of year**.
Turn coding club into **building with AI**.
feel: **Uneasy** in a mostly good way, like having a **runway**.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a runway for a teacher my age.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **career plan**.
He's ready to spend **half his savings** on a master's.
His mum, a former **dinner lady**, is the person he'd tell first.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in education and technology
Turn Wednesday coding club into building projects with AI
Shorten the summer trip to Italy to one week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be idiots to waste it. I'd want teacher unions and governments to agree a ten-year plan for schools. Online I'd be the optimistic one, which is my natural setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'm thirty-seven when it arrives, probably a head of year or deputy head. That's a people job, about behaviour and families and staff, and I think that's the last bit to go. I think I'm actually in a good place in this world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the master's at a normal pace and aim for head of year within four years. I'd save for a deposit, maybe buy a small flat with my partner around 2030. I'd use the tools every day, like now, and help write the school's policy on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worry left in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids. My Year 9s would be leaving university around 2036, right when it lands. I'd want to teach them how to work alongside AI and how to argue with it, not just how to code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a partner for the first time. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, sorry, I'm seeing someone, Nadia, who's a junior doctor. We're not living together yet, but a ten-year runway makes it easier to plan for that. With two years I wouldn't plan anything; with ten, I'd plan a life.

say: I'd call **ten years** a gift we can't afford to waste.
I'd want unions and government to agree a **ten-year plan** for schools.
think: By 2036 I'd likely be a **head of year** or deputy head.
People jobs about **behaviour and families** are the last to go.
do: Finish the **master's** at a normal pace and aim for head of year.
Save for a deposit and **buy a flat** with my partner around 2030.
S4.quote: With two years I wouldn't plan anything; with ten, I'd plan a life.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him picture a **senior people role** by 2036.
He reveals a **partner** only when the long timeline makes plans possible.
His remaining worry is for **his students**, who graduate as it lands.

steps.text: Finish the master's over three years and apply for head of year
Help write Eastfield Academy's policy on AI tools
Save for a deposit to buy a flat with Nadia

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd starve, I'd find something, but because schools would be thrown into chaos and the kids in front of me would pay for it. What would help is the government funding a national retraining scheme for teachers and protecting class sizes, so the money saved goes into more adults in schools, not fewer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the students think. My Year 10s talk about AI more than any adult I know, and some of them are already scared. Somebody should interview them.

headlineQuote: I'd want my mum to know I'm not quitting, I'm changing what kind of teacher I am.
portrait: Carlos is a second-year **computing teacher** at a large secondary who uses AI daily.
He rents a room in a **shared house**, has about four months saved, and leans left.
He sees **his own subject** as exposed early, but expects to adapt through pastoral work.
His mood moves from **calm** in the plateau to **anxious** with AGI in 2028, then back with time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because schools would be thrown into **chaos** and students would pay.
whatWouldHelp: Protected **class sizes** so savings go into more adults in schools.
